article_title: The Impact of Healthy Harlem on the Prevalence of Child Overweight and Obesity and Contributing Factors: Interim Evaluation Report
citation: Mabli, J., Bleeker, M., & Fox, M. K. (2017). The Impact of Healthy Harlem on the Prevalence of Child Overweight and Obesity and Contributing Factors: Interim Evaluation Report. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Universal prevention plus targeted intensive goal-setting tier for students needing additional support
description: The program combines a universal tier delivered to all participants with an intensive targeted tier for students identified as needing more support. All students are exposed to Prevention, "which includes physical activity, healthy snacks, nutrition education lessons, and parent workshops," while students who are overweight or obese "also participate in Get Fit, an intensive, 12-week program in which students identify and work on specific goals." This layered structure lets a broad educational base coexist with individualized goal work for a higher-need subgroup.
requirements: A universal delivery setting reaching all students (here, after-school programs)
A criterion for identifying students for the intensive tier (here, overweight or obesity status)
constraints: The intensive tier is limited to middle and high school students who are overweight or obese and runs for a fixed 12-week period
target_learners: All students in an after-school program, plus a targeted subgroup of middle and high school students who are overweight or obese
target_learning_goals: Nutrition knowledge and attitudes
Goal-setting for improving eating and physical-activity habits
examples: HCZ after-school students all received Prevention; those overweight or obese additionally received Get Fit, and the evaluation found BMI reductions for students receiving both components

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Researchers should take time to understand a digital learning platform's learning environment and capabilities before planning research within it
description: The report's first consideration holds that researchers must conduct due diligence on a DLP before planning studies, because research must fit within learning environments that already exist. Researchers should inquire about the learning setting, theory of action, typical implementation, and available content, since "researchers will need to be prepared to explore, modify, and study their ideas within learning environments that already exist." This saves the expense of building a platform while requiring creativity in fitting research interests to it.
requirements: Time investment in an information-gathering stage to determine alignment between research interests and the platform's learning opportunities
constraints: Researchers may need to be more innovative or creative in conceptualizing how their research interests fit within an existing environment rather than building new tools
target_learners: Education researchers considering studies within digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Aligning research questions with platform learning opportunities and capabilities
examples: SEERNet offers a Guide to Doing Research on DLPs, and the AIMS Collaboratory is creating a searchable catalog of researcher-ready DLPs covering grade level, content area, and type of research supported
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
citation: UNESCO. (2022). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org
title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence as a global standard instrument
description: The Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence is UNESCO's first global standard-setting instrument on AI ethics, adopted in 2021 and applicable to all 194 UNESCO member states. title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students: 12 competencies across four dimensions and three progression levels

citation: Miao, Fengchun; Cukurova, Mutlu. (2024). AI competency framework for teachers. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org
title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers: 15 competencies across five dimensions
description: The AI Competency Framework for Teachers defines "the knowledge, skills, and values teachers must master in the age of AI." It organizes teacher AI competence into "15 competencies across five dimensions": Human-centred mindset, Ethics of AI, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI for professional learning. article_title: College Prep for All? What We've Learned from Chicago's Efforts
citation: Elaine Allensworth, Takako Nomi, Nicholas Montgomery, & Valerie E. Lee. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Universal college-preparatory mandates need instructional supports, not just course requirements, to improve outcomes
description: The article argues that simply mandating rigorous courses for all is insufficient: schools attempting detracking face parent resistance, technical difficulties teaching heterogeneous classrooms, and low teacher expectations. It concludes that "a policy of universalizing college-preparatory courses may have little chance of success if it does not address such issues as professional development around instruction, widespread support for the policy among the school community (teachers and parents), and extra support for low-ability students." The Chicago evaluation bears this out: enrollment changed, but achievement did not.
requirements: Professional development around instruction, school-community support, and extra support courses for struggling students accompany the mandate
constraints: The article notes successful detracking schools appear exceptional, with shared belief in diversity and inclusive pedagogical practices
target_learners: all ninth graders, including low-ability and special education students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: success in college-preparatory coursework in place of remedial tracks
examples: Chicago mandated Algebra I and English I for all ninth graders in 1997 without the accompanying instructional supports the literature identifies, and test scores and college entrance did not improve

College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. citation: Schachner, A., Wang, V., Yun, C., Plasencia, S., Mauerman, C., McJunkins, C., & Stipek, D. (2025). Preparing early childhood teachers: Credentialing and preparation programs in four states. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/177.512
title: Design early childhood preparation programs around a unified vision, deep grounding in child development, and integrated coursework with field experiences

The report states that "Integrating coursework and field-based experiences makes for a more powerful learning experience" and that a unified vision "enables success." pedagogical skill for preschool through early elementary teaching

article_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Qualitative UNESCO Framework Analysis
citation: Adarkwah, M. A., Ercan, A. M., Schneider, K., & Bayar, E. (2026). Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Qualitative UNESCO Framework Analysis. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/801ryw41
title: UNESCO's eight-component GenAI framework as an evaluation lens for higher education GenAI policy robustness
description: UNESCO's eight-component GenAI framework is an evaluative framework whose components span ethical and governance principles as well as inclusion, equity, and sustainability considerations such as internet access, gender parity in AI, and environmental impact. The study uses it as "a lens for evaluating the robustness of the policies" of thirty highly ranked universities, scoring how fully each institution's GenAI policy covers the framework's elements. Coverage of the components varied widely across countries and institutions.

constraints: The framework was applied to highly ranked universities in the top ten countries for AI preparedness, not to all higher education institutions

promotion of academic integrity
examples: The study evaluated the GenAI policies of thirty QS-ranked universities across the top ten countries for AI preparedness using the framework's eight components

article_title: Understanding the Implementation of Universal FAFSA Completion Policies in Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, and Louisiana
citation: Victoria Jackson, Kyla Hurns, and Paulina Fraser. (2026). Understanding the Implementation of Universal FAFSA Completion Policies in Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, and Louisiana. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Three-component design framework for universal FAFSA completion policies
description: The report organizes state universal FAFSA policy design around three main components: "who is responsible for fulfilling the requirement, whether an opt-out waiver is available, and whether funding is provided to local education agencies (LEAs)." States also differ in whether policies were created through regulation or statute and in statewide supports promoting college enrollment. The framework is used to compare Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, and Louisiana, whose policies vary across all three components — from Colorado's funded competitive grant program to Indiana's and Louisiana's unfunded requirements.
requirements: A policy design must specify responsibility for the requirement, opt-out waiver availability, and whether LEA funding is provided
constraints: Louisiana and New Hampshire have repealed their policies, showing design choices affect policy durability
target_learning_goals: completing the FAFSA to access federal, state, and institutional financial aid
examples: Colorado's House Bill 21-1330 created the Fund My Future competitive grant program with an opt-out provision; Illinois' HB 2719 took effect for the class of 2021 with no appropriated funds

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence and the marginalization of minoritized knowledges in higher education
citation: Fatiha TALI OTMANI. (2025). L'intelligence artificielle générative et la marginalisation des savoirs minoritaires dans l'enseignement supérieur. Le cas du handicap. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22marginalisation+des+savoirs+minoritaires+dans+l%27enseignement+sup%C3%A9rieur%22
title: L'« usager universel » : figure normée de l'utilisateur qui exclut structurellement les étudiants en situation de handicap de la conception des outils d'IA
description: La revue mobilise le concept d'« usager universel » (Oudshoorn et al., 2004), via le cadre analytique de Collin et Marceau (2022), pour saisir l'exclusion des étudiants en situation de handicap. Ce concept « désigne la tendance des concepteurs à élaborer leurs outils pour un utilisateur implicitement normé, à savoir jeune, valide, occidental, maîtrisant une langue dominante, disposant d'un accès aisé aux infrastructures numériques ». Les étudiants en situation de handicap se trouvent exclus « non parce que les concepteurs les auraient oubliés délibérément, mais parce que leur situation les rend moins visibles dans les données et moins compatibles avec les catégories préexistantes ». Ce cadre articule les biais des systèmes d'IAG aux inégalités préexistantes.
requirements: Sortir de ce paradigme suppose, selon l'article, une recherche participative « impliquant les personnes concernées dans la conception et l'évaluation des outils d'IA éducative ».
constraints: L'article précise que la représentation des personnes en situation de handicap dans les équipes de conception « reste marginale, ce qui limite la capacité de ces équipes à anticiper les besoins et à éviter les biais d'exclusion ».
target_learners: étudiants en situation de handicap dans l'enseignement supérieur
target_learning_goals: conception d'outils d'IA éducative accessibles et adaptés à la diversité des situations de handicap
examples: Les architectures des outils d'IA sont conçues pour un utilisateur implicitement normé ; les outils conçus pour les utilisateurs « universels » se révèlent peu accessibles aux personnes présentant certains handicaps.
key_sources: Fatiha TALI OTMANI. (2025). L'intelligence artificielle générative et la marginalisation des savoirs minoritaires dans l'enseignement supérieur. Le cas du handicap. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22marginalisation+des+savoirs+minoritaires+dans+l%27enseignement+sup%C3%A9rieur%22

article_title: AI Anxiety: A Comprehensive Analysis of Psychological Factors and Interventions
citation: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9
title: Mitigate rising AI Anxiety by first understanding its root causes and then implementing strategic interventions
description: The article closes its abstract with a design principle for anyone responding to AI Anxiety: diagnosis precedes intervention. It states that "Understanding the root causes of AI Anxiety and implementing strategic interventions are critical steps for mitigating its rise as society enters the era of pervasive AI." The principle directs educators and designers to analyse which causes of anxiety operate in their population before selecting interventions, consistent with the article's cause-taxonomy-then-solutions structure. It frames both steps as critical rather than optional.

constraints: The article presents this as a critical step within its broader argument; the accessible text reports no test of the principle's effectiveness
target_learners: Educators, institutions, and policymakers designing responses to AI Anxiety among learners and workers
target_learning_goals: Mitigating AI Anxiety as AI becomes pervasive in learning and work contexts
examples: The article's own sequence: examining psychological factors underlying AI Anxiety before proposing solutions to tackle the problem

title: Universities as socio-technical systems in which human and technological components jointly shape student communication
description: The article frames chatbot implementation through the lens of universities as socio-technical systems, in which "human and technological components are intertwined and jointly shape organizational processes." Effective student communication depends on coordination across administrative units, access to shared data, and the ability to adapt institutional processes over time, not on the technology alone. article_title: Mind the Student: Behavioral and Contextual Cues for Automated Engagement Prediction in Online Learning
citation: Alperen Kantarcı, Visvanathan Ramesh, and Gemma Roig. 2026. Mind the Student: Behavioral and Contextual Cues for Automated Engagement Prediction in Online Learning. ICMI '26, Napoli, Italy. https://doi.org/10.1145/3776574.3832485
title: Evaluate engagement-prediction methods by uncertainty handling and generalization, not predictive accuracy alone, and deploy them only as research tools
description: Because engagement prediction in ambiguous regimes can be near-random, the authors argue methods "should be evaluated not only by predictive accuracy, but also by how well they handle uncertainty, exploit multimodal structure, and generalize to unseen students". Their own system operationalizes this by reporting calibrated epistemic uncertainty alongside predictions. They further caution that the system "is intended as a research tool for understanding engagement dynamics, not as a surveillance or performance evaluation instrument for deployed educational settings".
requirements: Uncertainty metrics (e.g., epistemic uncertainty from evidential or GP heads) reported alongside accuracy metrics
Student-independent evaluation protocols to test generalization to unseen students
constraints: The authors state the system may exhibit performance disparities across demographic groups not well-represented in the relatively small training cohort
The intended use is research understanding of engagement dynamics, not surveillance or performance evaluation in deployed educational settings
target_learning_goals: reliable, uncertainty-aware automated engagement prediction for educational research tools
examples: The authors benchmarked their framework on the CASED challenge test set under a strict student-independent protocol, reporting F1, MCC, RMSE, and CCC alongside uncertainty metrics

article_title: Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models
citation: Jiajia Song, Zhihan Guo, and Jionghao Lin. (2026). Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26142
title: Knowledge-level student simulation pipeline: machine unlearning to initialize a stable novice state, then supervised and coach-guided relearning to model growth under tutoring
description: This framework replaces prompt-only role assignment with model-level knowledge degradation for LLM teachable agents. It argues that "prompt-based role assignment does not alter the model's underlying pre-trained knowledge, often leading to expert knowledge leakage and unstable role fidelity". The pipeline runs in three stages: machine unlearning of targeted knowledge components via LoRA, controlled relearning via supervised fine-tuning on forgotten QA pairs, and instructional relearning in a three-agent teachable-agent environment where a coach agent gives corrective feedback used as training signals.
requirements: A curated dataset with concept labels so unlearning targets can be drawn at knowledge-component and question levels
A capable full-knowledge coach LLM to deliver corrective feedback during instructional relearning
constraints: Experiments used only Python MCQs and a single base language model, which the authors state may limit generalisability to other subjects, task formats, or model architectures
The method operates at the level of knowledge representations and may not capture complex cognitive and social factors in human learning, such as affective processes
target_learners: Human students acting as tutors in learning-by-teaching settings
Teachers and tutors in practice-based professional development

citation: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. title: Unicode perturbation families implemented as system-prompt soft barriers
description: The paper implements soft barriers as a system prompt instructing the model to inject specific Unicode characters into user-defined identifiers during generation, leaving keywords, operators, literals, and built-in names unchanged. title: Uncanny Valley Theory as a boundary condition on agent realism in immersive learning environments
description: The review invokes Uncanny Valley Theory (Mori et al., 2012) as a risk qualifier for the otherwise positive effects of heightened agent realism. According to the review, "agents with increasing realism are perceived positively at first and enjoy greater trust, but if the similarity to real people exceeds a certain threshold and reaches the 'uncanny valley' this leads to a sudden rejection." Only when the valley is overcome does perception become positive again. The review states many studies over the last decade have shown this effect and its neurophysiological correlates, and concludes that designers must ensure realism quality does not fall into the uncanny valley when building sound human-agent spaces in immersive environments.
requirements: Agent realism quality must be managed so that similarity to real people does not fall into the uncanny valley
constraints: The effect is described as occurring only when similarity to real people exceeds a certain threshold

article_title: The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments
citation: Matthew Inglis, Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2008). The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments.
title: Uncertainty-gated authority model of argument evaluation
description: The article proposes a model (illustrated in its Figure 2) in which "the source of an argument only influences the reader's reported level of persuasion if, having read the argument, the reader is left uncertain about it" — that is, an authority figure can only operate on existing uncertainty. It accounts for the heuristic argument (uncertainty present, authority effect found), the formal proofs (little uncertainty, no effect), and the visual argument (students certain it was unacceptable, researchers uncertain, so only researchers showed the effect). The authors note it also predicts authority effects when an argument is too hard to understand or effort is not invested, though this was not tested.
requirements: The reader must be left with some uncertainty about the argument's mathematical status after reading it for authority to influence persuasion
constraints: The authors state the model's prediction about difficulty and time restrictions creating uncertainty has not been tested

target_learning_goals: evaluating the persuasiveness of mathematical arguments
gaining conviction in mathematical statements
examples: The model explains why Gowers's heuristic argument showed an authority effect while the induction and Pólya formal proofs did not

article_title: Reverse-correlation reveals internal error-corrections during information-seeking
citation: Lorenz Weise, Saskia D. Forster, Siegfried Gauggel. (2022). Reverse-correlation reveals internal error-corrections during information-seeking. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:321–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09286-4
title: Unitary confidence mechanism supporting the isomechanism view of metacognitive monitoring
description: The article advances the account that different ways of expressing confidence reflect one underlying inferential process rather than specialized processes. It states that "a unitary confidence mechanism was able to explain behavioral results in all three conditions without distinguishing between the three forms of assessing confidence", which "speaks to the isomechanism position". The mechanism is a signal-detection-style decision-and-confidence model in which low-confidence trials trigger a second internal signal sample; allowing internal error-corrections explains why info-seeking yields inverted decision weights while explicit reports and wagering do not.

target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of decision confidence
examples: Fitting the signal-detection-based decision-and-confidence model to each participant's reverse-correlation decision weights from all three confidence-assessment conditions

citation: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6
title: Unconscious self-regulation via resonant states in sensory memory that trigger automatized strategy use without working-memory resources
description: Citing Wirth, Stebner, Trypke, Schuster, and Leutner, the review presents a new perspective in which self-regulation can be not only conscious but unconscious. "They introduce the so-called resonant states in sensory memory which trigger a bottom-up and top-down interaction, where external stimuli are aligned with expectations." A material feature, such as text without subsections, can match an expectation of a difficult text and automatically start a strategy like underlining and note taking without reaching consciousness, so it does not require working-memory resources. This account implies the cognitive costs of self-regulation can be eliminated when learning strategies are highly automatized.
requirements: Learners need substantial self-regulation knowledge and expertise: they must know which text features indicate complexity and which strategy is functional, and be able to apply the strategy without attentional control from working memory
constraints: The trigger needs a fruitful ground for resonance, so the account applies to learners with automatized strategies rather than novices

target_learning_goals: Automatic initiation of appropriate learning strategies without consuming working-memory resources
examples: A text without subsections or paragraphs matching the expectation of a difficult text automatically triggers underlining and note taking

title: Universities as defensible spaces: a territorial, surveilled, and symbolic space framework
description: The article adapts Newman's Defensible Space Theory—originally a model for residential environments that 'inhibits crime by creating the physical expression of a social fabric that defends itself'—to university campuses. It proposes that campuses are (1) territorial, (2) surveilled, and (3) symbolic spaces, and that these features sharpen ingroup-outgroup boundaries and reify racial and class disparities, leaving marginalized students feeling like trespassers. title: Incorporate unproctored exams together with pre-exam integrity reminders into university assessment practices to reduce cheating
description: The article concludes that "incorporating unproctored exams and pre-exam academic integrity reminders into a university's assessment practices may be a useful strategy for reducing academic dishonesty and upholding assessment validity." Across four double-blind randomized field experiments and a mini-meta-analysis, the unproctored (trust exam) format outperformed teacher-proctored exams on both cheating rate and cheating extent, and reminders added an independent rate reduction. The principle rests on a university population experienced with unproctored exams.
requirements: Students should be familiar with the unproctored exam process and academic integrity expectations; at the study university, 10% of exams were unproctored and students had decades of institutional experience with the Trust Exam system
constraints: The exam-format effect on cheating rate was not significant in Study 3 when reminders were present, though the pooled analysis favored the unproctored format
Findings come from second-year undergraduates at one Chinese university without an honor code system
target_learning_goals: reducing academic dishonesty and upholding assessment validity
examples: Students from the same class were randomly assigned within double-blind field experiments to unproctored or proctored conditions, with professors and students unaware of assigned conditions before the exam

article_title: Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view
citation: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005
title: Unpacked simple view of reading: oral comprehension comprises lower level language skills and discourse skills as dissociable dimensions
description: The study refines the simple view of reading by unpacking its oral comprehension component. Rather than one broad oral language factor, the article reports that "lower level language skills (vocabulary, syntax) and discourse skills (oral text comprehension) emerged as two dimensions of 'oral comprehension'". LLL skills cover vocabulary breadth and syntactic skills assessed at word and sentence level, while discourse skills cover comprehension of whole oral texts requiring inference-making and integration. The framework was operationalised in longitudinal structural equation models predicting end-of-first-grade reading comprehension in French.
requirements: Assessment must separately measure vocabulary, syntax, and oral text comprehension rather than aggregating them, since sentence-level and text-level interpretation "might not involve similar cognitive mechanisms".
constraints: The two factors were highly correlated (.81 at T1, .73 at T2), and the structure was established in French first-graders, a moderately transparent orthography.
target_learners: First-grade pupils (around 6 years old) learning to read in French
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension development
Oral language comprehension
examples: Confirmatory factor analyses at T1 and T2 with 556 pupils compared three-factor models against two-factor alternatives, favouring the three-factor structure at both time points.

article_title: The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary?
citation: M.M.L. Muijselaar, N.M. Swart, E.G. Steenbeek-Planting, M. Droop, L. Verhoeven, P.F. de Jong. (2017). The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary? Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(1), 70-83. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000120
title: Unidimensional account of reading comprehension
description: The article advances the account that reading comprehension, as measured across varying texts and question types, is best described by a single general factor rather than multiple specific dimensions. Its analyses found specific measures "hardly reflected systematic variation" once a general factor was modeled, so items "largely reflect a common factor". This account challenges the frequent implicit assumption that reading comprehension is multidimensional.
requirements: Requires item pools sampling different text and question types so that specific dimensions, if present, could emerge in factor models
constraints: Evidence comes from Dutch fourth-grade children and the item pool and text/question types studied
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
examples: Multitrait, multimethod and confirmatory factor models applied to the administered item pool

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--IV.
citation: Colvin, S. S., & Pintner, R. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Intelligence testing should include untimed tests emphasizing deliberation, analysis, synthesis, and extended attention span
description: Colvin recommends developing test elements that emphasize deliberation and sustained rational ability, in which speed is relatively unimportant and analysis, synthesis, and an extensive attention span are the chief factors. He argues current tests overemphasize speed and that tests of higher intellectual processes are needed in greater degree than simple tests of facts, memory, and perception. As he puts it, "we need at present test elements that emphasize, more than any now existing do, deliberation and substained rational ability."
requirements: Tests must give the individual who thinks carefully, accurately, but sometimes ponderously, an opportunity to show his ability.
constraints: Colvin notes pioneer work on such tests had been done by Thorndike, particularly in his tests for college freshmen, indicating such tests were not yet standard.
target_learners: students from primary grades through college taking intelligence tests
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of higher intellectual processes and learning capacity
examples: Colvin cites Thorndike's tests for college freshmen as pioneer work emphasizing deliberation rather than speed.

article_title: The power of the eye to sustain clear seeing under different conditions of lighting.
citation: C. E. Ferree and Gertrude Rand. (1917). The Power of the Eye to Sustain Clear Seeing Under Different Conditions of Lighting. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Install lighting so that the field of vision is uniformly illuminated, well diffused, and free of extremes of surface brightness, because distribution factors govern the eye's comfort and efficiency
description: The article's central design recommendation for lighting spaces used for sustained visual work: the ideal condition is to have the field of vision "uniformly illuminated with light well diffused and no extremes of surface brightness," since such gradation of retinal illumination supports accurate and comfortable fixation and accommodation. The authors derive this from six years of tests showing distribution factors are fundamental to the eye's welfare, and they rank lighting systems by how well they realize it.
requirements: Light sources concealed or diffused so no extremes of surface brightness enter the field of view
Bright sources kept out of the zone of most harmful influence on the eye, easiest in rooms with higher ceilings
constraints: In rooms of low or medium height, protecting the eye is the most difficult feature of the problem; the difficulty decreases with increase in the height of the ceiling
target_learners: students and workers doing sustained reading or visual work in artificially and daylit rooms
target_learning_goals: sustaining clear seeing and visual comfort during prolonged reading and study
examples: The authors report the best control of the distribution factors in daylight rooms and, among artificial systems, in indirect and high-density semi-indirect installations

article_title: Shared and distinct neural correlates of first and second language morphological processing in bilingual brain
citation: Fei Gao, Lin Hua, Paulo Armada-da-Silva, Juan Zhang, Defeng Li, Zhiyi Chen, Chengwen Wang, Meng Du, Zhen Yuan. (2023). Shared and distinct neural correlates of first and second language morphological processing in bilingual brain. npj Science of Learning 8:33. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00184-9
title: Unified competition model of bilingual development applied to morphological processing
description: The unified competition model holds that for language structures shared between L1 and L2, bilinguals employ common cognitive resources and strategies drawn from L1. The article frames its findings as supporting this account: "the current results support a uni ﬁed competition model for bilingual development, where bilinguals would primarily employ L1 neural resources for L2 morphological representation and processing." Shared ELAN, P250 and LAN patterns across L1 and L2, plus quantitative (not qualitative) L1–L2 frontal differences, are cited as evidence of L1-to-L2 resource transfer.
requirements: L1 and L2 must share the linguistic structure under investigation (here derivational morphology)
constraints: The article notes it cannot completely rule out the proficiency confounding effect on current results, since participants' English proficiency was below Chinese by no means addressed with monolingual controls
Evidence comes from late bilinguals with intermediate-to-high English proficiency, so generalization to early bilinguals is open
target_learners: late bilinguals at intermediate to advanced L2 proficiency
target_learning_goals: L2 morphological representation and processing
cross-language transfer of morphological parsing strategies
examples: Chinese-English bilinguals performed a visual derivational morphological priming task while EEG and fNIRS were recorded simultaneously; L1 and L2 shared early and late structural parsing processes
The study did not find dissociable brain regions for L1 and L2 morphological processing, only quantitative left-frontal differences

citation: Fabian Santiago-Muñoz, Mikel Larrañaga, Jon A. Elorriaga, Ana Arruarte. (2025). Identification of Patterns to Prevent the Failure of Engineering Students. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35:3356–3405. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00502-9
title: Exploratory unsupervised clustering methodology for identifying at-risk student profiles from pre-admission data
description: The article develops an exploratory, unsupervised methodology that applies clustering to university pre-admission data to find latent structures without predefined labels. "The process involves three main phases (see Fig. 1): Data Preparation, Experimentation and Analysis of the Selected Models." Model selection combines internal validation (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz), association with outcomes (Cramér's V), and cluster quality (purity, entropy) via a composite score. It is positioned as an alternative to deductive, theory-driven and supervised approaches.
requirements: Requires the necessary educational data to be available, as the article states the methodology is applicable to other subjects as long as such data exist
Requires sequential filtering with explicit thresholds (Silhouette > 0; Cramér's V > 0.3)
constraints: Applicable to other subjects only as long as the necessary educational data are available
Results depend on the choice of normalization technique

citation: Dabae Lee. (2021). The process of designing for [online] learning: response to Bennett et al.. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09915-w
title: Understanding faculty design practices is critical for supporting the transfer of instruction online
description: The article argues that institutions cannot effectively support faculty moving to online teaching without first understanding how those faculty actually design instruction. article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: United reflection model combining deliberate and aware epistemological perspectives
description: The article proposes a united reflection model in which six reflective processes are derived by crossing three types of reflection (on, for, in action) with two epistemological perspectives. The deliberate perspective involves "Knowledge-based processing by focusing on evidence-based norms" while the aware perspective involves "Context-based processing by focusing on salient moments". Uniting them is claimed to yield better sense-making, better instructional planning, and more responsive teaching, with each reflection type producing a complete picture to guide understanding, planning, or in-the-moment adjustment.
requirements: Teachers engage in reflection activities spanning both deliberate analysis against standards and explication of practical awareness
Reflection is structured across retrospective, anticipatory, and in-action temporal foci
constraints: The model is a theoretical proposal; the article presents no empirical test of it
target_learning_goals: Contextualized knowledge of how to teach
Reflective practice
Instructional planning
examples: The article maps RoA, RfA, and RiA onto Bloom's revised taxonomy complexity levels and summarizes the six processes in Fig. 2

article_title: Toward a framework of uncertainty in ill-structured problem solving
citation: Rebecca Clark-Stallkamp, Barbara B. Lockee. (2026). Toward a framework of uncertainty in ill-structured problem solving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10680-5
title: A framework of uncertainty in ill-structured problem solving: a subjective locus plus seven intersecting sources
description: The framework defines uncertainty as a subjective, metacognitive and psychological experience — the locus of uncertainty, "a psychological response or subjective state of unknowingness" — arising as learners interpret problems, make judgments, and regulate action under incomplete, conflicting, or changing information. Around this locus it delineates seven intersecting sources: problem context/space, outcomes, sociocultural, epistemological, environmental, dynamicity, and complexity. Complexity and dynamicity act as overarching amplifiers, and all sources are situated within the problem context, which serves as the foundation for how uncertainty manifests. The framework was derived from thematic and taxonomic coding of 74 peer-reviewed articles.
requirements: Articles in the underlying corpus had to describe a problem or decision-making context, connect to learning or knowledge construction, and explicitly reference uncertainty or evidence of it manifesting
constraints: Derived from literature coded by the first author with second-author auditing rather than dual coding; intended for ill-structured problem-solving and learning contexts
target_learning_goals: problem solving
metacognitive regulation of uncertainty
argumentation and justification of solutions
examples: Taxonomic coding of the 74-article corpus produced the seven source categories and the locus of uncertainty, with code examples tabulated for each component

article_title: The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments
citation: Ozcelik, E., Ercil Cagiltay, N., & Sahin Ozcelik, N. (2013). The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments. Computers & Education, 67, 12–20. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.02.009
title: Research model linking uncertainty, motivation, accuracy, response time, and learning outcomes
description: The article proposes a hypothesized causal model (Fig. 2) of relationships between uncertainty, motivation, accuracy, response time, and post-test performance, operationalized in seven hypotheses (H1–H7). The model holds that "uncertainty is positively related to motivation", motivation relates to accuracy and response time during learning, and all four relate positively to the post-test. A path analysis using LISREL 8.8 tested the model with adequate fit (GFI = 0.95, CFI = 0.92, SRMR = 0.05), and the model accounted for 20% of the variance in the post-test.
requirements: Testing requires behavioral measures (accuracy, response time), motivation scores, and post-test scores collected during game play
constraints: The model was tested in a single game-like environment teaching Entity-Relationship Diagram concepts in higher education
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer engineering, software engineering, and information systems engineering
target_learning_goals: database design concepts (Entity-Relationship Diagrams)

title: Uniview fulldome virtual tour of Solar System moons at Gates Planetarium
description: An instructional visualization element in which "the UniviewTM planetarium software developed by the company SCISS AB was used to generate a virtual tour of the Solar System," presented by an instructor with a skilled navigator piloting the software in real time. The tour showed realistic moon and planet imagery (from telescopic and spacecraft data) either on a flat-screen classroom projection (GII) or as immersive visuals in the Denver Museum of Nature & Science's fulldome Gates Planetarium (GIII). The tour demonstrated tidal locking, visited each planet's satellites, highlighted non-co-planar orbits of outer-planet moons, and showed the Galilean orbital resonance via camera cuts.
requirements: A skilled navigator present to pilot the software following the lecture outline in real time
Imagery of surfaces captured by Earth-bound telescopes and visiting spacecraft
constraints: The same lecture outline, instructors, and visuals were used across treatments to isolate the display format; no other animations were shown in any class
target_learning_goals: distinguishing moons from other objects, knowing moon counts and identities per planet, and understanding moon origins and orbital behaviors
examples: The tour started with Earth's Moon's tidal locking, noted Mercury and Venus have no satellites, identified Mars' moons as likely captured asteroids, and explored Jupiter through Neptune's satellites in turn
key_sources: Yu, K. C., Sahami, K., Denn, G., Sahami, V., & Sessions, L. C. (2016). Immersive Planetarium Visualizations for Teaching Solar System Moon Concepts to Undergraduates. Journal of Astronomy & Earth Sciences Education, 3(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1123383

article_title: Fadeout in an Early Mathematics Intervention: Same Old Schools or Underlying Skills?
citation: Bailey, D. H., Nguyen, T., Jenkins, J. M., Domina, T., Clements, D. H., Sarama, J., Wolfe, C. B., & Spitler, M. E. (2015). Fadeout in an Early Mathematics Intervention: Same Old Schools or Underlying Skills? SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563521
title: Underlying skills hypothesis of fadeout
description: The underlying skills hypothesis proposes that short-run achievement gains from early interventions are eventually overtaken by relatively stable factors — domain general cognitive abilities, stable academic skills, motivation — shaping long-term mathematical development. It predicts that control children reaching the same post-intervention score without treatment are advantaged on underlying skills and will show greater subsequent gains. The article's matched-sample results support this account over the same old schools hypothesis.
requirements: Requires longitudinal follow-up assessment after intervention conclusion to test whether trajectories revert to levels predicted by underlying skills
constraints: Tested here only for an effective early mathematics intervention (Building Blocks/TRIAD) in low-resource schools
target_learning_goals: early mathematics achievement
examples: Matched control children outperformed matched treatment children at follow-up (p < .001), consistent with this hypothesis
key_sources: Bailey, D. H., Nguyen, T., Jenkins, J. M., Domina, T., Clements, D. H., Sarama, J., Wolfe, C. B., & Spitler, M. E. (2015). Fadeout in an Early Mathematics Intervention: Same Old Schools or Underlying Skills? SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562173

article_title: The myth that slow test-takers are worse students: Implications for time-limited testing.
citation: Weiner Saul J., Park Yoon Soo, Gernsbacher Morton Ann, Petersen Kristina H. (2026). The myth that slow test-takers are worse students: Implications for time-limited testing. Medical education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70215
title: Eliminate time limits on written high-stakes assessments by universalizing maximal accommodation
description: The commentary recommends eliminating speededness through untimed power testing, achieved by "giving all examinees maximum accommodation, which is typically double time." This immediately removes inequities in who applies for and obtains accommodation, resolves adverse validity effects, and reduces strain on students, schools and disability staff. The authors recommend eliminating time limits expeditiously, arguing the question is why high-stakes exams have not already done so.
requirements: Exam formats and logistics must be adjusted so all examinees receive maximal accommodation time, typically double time
constraints: Practical simulation tests assessing performance where time is part of the construct, such as responding to cardiac arrest, should remain time-limited
target_learning_goals: accurate and equitable assessment of medical knowledge and clinical reasoning
examples: The commentary proposes universalizing maximal accommodation as a first step, noting it would eliminate inequities related to who applies for accommodation
key_sources: Weiner Saul J., Park Yoon Soo, Gernsbacher Morton Ann, Petersen Kristina H. (2026). The myth that slow test-takers are worse students: Implications for time-limited testing. Medical education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70215

article_title: Effectiveness of a novel pork belly simulation model versus traditional training for ultrasound-guided TAP block in anesthesiology residents.
citation: Cheng Sipei, Zeng Helin, Kang Yanming, Wu Lan, Chen Shouming. (2026). Effectiveness of a novel pork belly simulation model versus traditional training for ultrasound-guided TAP block in anesthesiology residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09546-4
title: Calibration of self-perception in traditional clinical training: transition from unconscious to conscious incompetence
description: The authors interpret the observed decrease in equipment preparation self-ratings in the traditional training group as "a result of a calibration of self-perception" rather than declining ability. Residents observing experienced operators "may realize that they were not as proficient in independent operation as they had imagined", leading to more conservative post-training self-ratings. The authors frame this as "a normal psychological process of transitioning from 'unconscious incompetence' to 'conscious incompetence' in skill acquisition theory". In contrast, the simulation model required residents to perform all steps independently, building self-efficacy through repeated hands-on practice.
requirements: Opportunity for residents to observe experienced operators in clinical settings
constraints: This interpretation is offered as an explanation for observed self-rating changes, not as a directly tested finding
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of procedural competence
professional identity development
examples: Group A residents' equipment preparation self-ratings decreased from 4.0 to 3.0 after traditional clinical training, which the authors attribute to calibration rather than skill decline
key_sources: Cheng Sipei, Zeng Helin, Kang Yanming, Wu Lan, Chen Shouming. (2026). Effectiveness of a novel pork belly simulation model versus traditional training for ultrasound-guided TAP block in anesthesiology residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09546-4

article_title: University teachers' self-efficacy beliefs.
citation: Douwes‐van Ark, I. M. E., Fokkens‐Bruinsma, M., Deinum, J. F., & Korpershoek, H. (2026). University teachers' self‐efficacy beliefs. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70088
title: UNITSS: a six-domain taxonomy of university teachers' self‐efficacy beliefs
description: The UNIversity Teaching Self‐Efficacy Scale (UNITSS) conceptualizes university teachers' self‐efficacy beliefs across six teaching domains: "creating a positive learning climate, instruction/design, differentiation, student engagement, assessment and professional development". It was built by adapting items from three prior instruments and adding items to cover each domain's conceptualization, with five to eight items per domain scored on a 5‐point Likert scale. The article uses it to profile teachers' efficacy levels and relate them to teacher characteristics.
requirements: Items per domain must reflect the domain's conceptualization; a thinking‐aloud procedure and pilot were used to ensure clarity
constraints: Design and instruction merged into one domain based on the EFA results
Robustness of the six domains requires confirmation in replication studies
target_learning_goals: Teaching self‐efficacy across six teaching domains
key_sources: Douwes‐van Ark, I. M. E., Fokkens‐Bruinsma, M., Deinum, J. F., & Korpershoek, H. (2026). University teachers' self‐efficacy beliefs. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70088

article_title: Executive functions and school achievement: The mediating role of learning-related behaviour in primary school children.
citation: Rivella, C., & Viterbori, P. (2025). Executive functions and school achievement: The mediating role of learning‐related behaviour in primary school children. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70053
title: Universal classroom interventions in the first grade should strengthen EF skills and promote learning-related behaviours together
description: The article recommends supporting early school success through universal classroom interventions that address both executive function weaknesses and LRBs, since EF relates to achievement partly through LRBs. The authors note "Recent research highlights the effectiveness of universal classroom interventions designed to enhance EF and self‐regulation in all children", and argue such whole-class approaches help because teachers struggle to identify children with poor EF absent a clinical diagnosis.
requirements: Requires teachers or schools to deliver EF and self-regulation activities to the whole class rather than targeting diagnosed children individually
constraints: Evidence base cited is from recent research the authors name (e.g., Diamond & Ling, 2020; Raver et al., 2011) rather than tested in this study
target_learning_goals: Early literacy and numeracy achievement
Classroom self-regulation and learning-related behaviours
examples: The article's Implications section proposes targeted interventions for WM and inhibition weaknesses plus support for LRBs such as attention control, persistence, and cooperation early in the school journey.
key_sources: Rivella, C., & Viterbori, P. (2025). Executive functions and school achievement: The mediating role of learning‐related behaviour in primary school children. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70053

article_title: Knowledge of Pressure Ulcers Amongst Nurses and Associated Factors: A Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Kocaslan Toran Meryem, Özgür Su, Aslan Fatma Eti, Toygar İsmail (2026). Knowledge of Pressure Ulcers Amongst Nurses and Associated Factors: A Cross‐Sectional Study. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.70888
title: Unit-specific, practice-based training strategies are recommended over generic ('one-size-fits-all') pressure injury education
description: The article recommends tailoring pressure injury education to the clinical risk profile of the nurse's work unit rather than delivering generic training to all nurses. It argues that because knowledge scores were highest in high-risk units such as operating rooms and lowest in outpatient clinics, "practise-based and unit-specific training should be increased, especially for nurses working outside high-risk areas such as operating rooms." The conclusion states these findings "support the need for targeted, unit-specific and practise‐based training strategies aligned with the clinical risk profile."
requirements: Education content should align with the clinical risk profile of the unit where the nurse works.
constraints: Recommendation rests on a cross-sectional survey design, which the authors state restricts causal inference and precludes evaluating the effects of educational interventions.
target_learners: Registered nurses and nurse supervisors in hospital clinical units
target_learning_goals: Pressure injury prevention knowledge, including risk assessment, staging and wound description
examples: In the study, operating-room nurses (median 47.50) significantly outscored outpatient-clinic nurses (median 39.50), motivating the call for targeted training outside high-risk areas.
key_sources: Kocaslan Toran Meryem, Özgür Su, Aslan Fatma Eti, Toygar İsmail (2026). Knowledge of Pressure Ulcers Amongst Nurses and Associated Factors: A Cross‐Sectional Study. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.70888

article_title: A serious video game for teaching basic point-of-care echocardiography skills: a non-inferiority trial.
citation: Lintschinger Josef Michael et al. (2026). A serious video game for teaching basic point-of-care echocardiography skills: a non-inferiority trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08995-1
title: Underwater serious video game for ultrasound hand-eye coordination training
description: Underwater (Sfinx Games, Groningen, Netherlands) is a serious video game in which learners "find objects in a playful underwater environment" using 3D-printed ultrasound probes, practicing probe manipulation and the probe-movement-to-image relationship. In this trial it served as the intervention tool in four 20-minute sessions, compared against a mannequin-based ultrasound simulator for basic cardiac POCUS hand-eye coordination in medical novices.
requirements: A 3D-printed ultrasound probe controller and the game software; participants practice locating hidden objects from predefined views
constraints: The game does not integrate learners into a comprehensive virtual clinical environment, limiting applicability for complex clinical decision-making or workflow-related skills
target_learners: Medical students with basic anatomy knowledge and no prior cardiac POCUS experience
target_learning_goals: Hand-eye coordination in ultrasound probe manipulation and basic cardiac POCUS image acquisition
examples: Used as the intervention in four 20-minute training sessions over two weeks in a randomized non-inferiority trial
key_sources: Lintschinger Josef Michael et al. (2026). A serious video game for teaching basic point-of-care echocardiography skills: a non-inferiority trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08995-1

article_title: Psychological quality and entrepreneurial competence: the mediating role of professional recognition and moderating effect of academic discipline among Chinese university students.
citation: Tian Qi, Huang Yinpin, Xiong Jun. (2026). Psychological quality and entrepreneurial competence: the mediating role of professional recognition and moderating effect of academic discipline among Chinese university students. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-03954-3
title: The "universal mediation, contextual activation" model of psychological quality and entrepreneurial competence
description: This model integrates Social Cognitive Theory with Self-Determination Theory and Becher and Trowler's "Academic Tribes" concept: psychological quality, a Positive Psychology-consistent resource profile of "self-efficacy, optimism, hope, and resilience", acts as a bottom-up personal resource that promotes entrepreneurial competence "mainly through the cognitive-affective pathways of professional recognition". The mediation mechanism is universal across disciplines, but the activation of professional recognition by psychological resources "is more sensitive in applied contexts", where problem-based and project-oriented pedagogy makes the personal-attribute-to-outcome link more tangible.
requirements: Measurement invariance across disciplinary groups before comparing structural paths, as the article establishes full metric invariance before multi-group testing
constraints: Findings derive from a cross-sectional self-report survey of undergraduates at four public science-and-technology-oriented universities in Hubei Province, China
target_learners: Chinese undergraduate university students across Humanities, Social Sciences, Natural Sciences and Engineering
target_learning_goals: Development of entrepreneurial competence (opportunity recognition, resource integration, innovation, setback tolerance)
examples: The study stratified 741 undergraduates into four disciplinary groups per Becher and Trowler's epistemic framework (Hard-Applied, Soft-Applied, Hard-Pure, Soft-Pure) and compared structural paths across groups
key_sources: Tian Qi, Huang Yinpin, Xiong Jun. (2026). Psychological quality and entrepreneurial competence: the mediating role of professional recognition and moderating effect of academic discipline among Chinese university students. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-03954-3

article_title: Pre- and in-service teachers attribution beliefs for students' success and struggle in mathematics: first insights.
citation: Ocal Tugba, Yavuz Selim, Ocal Mehmet Fatih. (2025). Pre- and in-service teachers attribution beliefs for students’ success and struggle in mathematics: first insights. BMC Psychology 13, 703. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03038-8
title: Understand teachers' attributional beliefs because they can shape instructional decisions and expectations
description: The article argues that teachers' beliefs about why students succeed or struggle in mathematics are consequential for practice: beliefs act as a cognitive filter guiding instructional decisions, classroom practices, and student learning. The study highlights "the importance of understanding teachers' beliefs, as these beliefs have the potential to shape instructional decisions and expectations." Teacher education and professional development should therefore attend to attributional beliefs, including whether they emphasize fixed innate ability or controllable factors.
requirements: Programs or researchers must elicit teachers' attributional beliefs, e.g., through interviews or validated instruments such as the AME framework
constraints: The study used convenience sampling, which the authors note limits generalizability and carries selection-bias risk
target_learners: pre-service and in-service elementary and middle school teachers
target_learning_goals: teachers' awareness of their attributional beliefs about students' mathematics success and struggle
examples: The study interviewed 28 teachers about why some students succeed in mathematics while others struggle and categorized their attributions into four types
key_sources: Ocal Tugba, Yavuz Selim, Ocal Mehmet Fatih. (2025). Pre- and in-service teachers attribution beliefs for students’ success and struggle in mathematics: first insights. BMC Psychology 13, 703. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03038-8

article_title: Promoting effective transitions: Primary school social-emotional competencies predict secondary school reading and numeracy achievement.
citation: Carpendale, E. J., Green, M. J., White, S. L. J., Williams, K. E., Tzoumakis, S., Watkeys, O. J., Harris, F., O'Hare, K., Carr, V. J., & Laurens, K. R. (2025). Promoting effective transitions: Primary school social–emotional competencies predict secondary school reading and numeracy achievement. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 496–512. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12735
title: Universally teach Self-Awareness and Self-Management during primary school to safeguard academic achievement across the transition to secondary school
description: The article recommends fostering students' intrapersonal social–emotional skills (Self-Awareness and Self-Management) in primary school, before the primary-to-secondary transition. Because effects were "common across reading and numeracy rather than domain‐specific", universal classroom delivery is proposed as a means of supporting achievement across curriculum areas. The conclusion endorses universally supporting social–emotional development, "particularly intrapersonal skills", as resources for learning into secondary school.
requirements: SEL teaching delivered universally in primary school (Year 6 or earlier) before the transition to secondary school
constraints: Effects after controlling for prior achievement and covariates were small (β .05–.15); the three interpersonal competencies showed no practically meaningful academic associations in this study
target_learners: Primary school students in their final years of primary school (middle childhood, ~age 11)
target_learning_goals: Maintaining reading and numeracy achievement across the primary-to-secondary transition
examples: The longitudinal study linked Year 6 MCS-SEL self-reports to Year 7 NAPLAN scores for 23,865 students, finding Self-Awareness and Self-Management significantly predicted both outcomes after covariate adjustment.

article_title: Teaching Procedural Skills: Integrating Educational Theory Into Practice.
citation: Smith Christopher J. MD, Rohlfsen Cory MD, Wardian Jana PhD, MSW, Sahak Khalid MD. (2024). Teaching Procedural Skills: Integrating Educational Theory Into Practice. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11476
title: 90-minute teach-the-teacher workshop on procedural skills teaching (University of Nebraska Medical Center clinician educator track)
description: A 90-minute interactive workshop for medical residents and fellows (postgraduate years 2–6) from 11 disciplines, developed as part of a clinician educator track. It integrated "Gagne's model of instructional design with evidence-based teaching practices" (Peyton's four-step model and deliberate practice), used small-group role-play applying Gagne's model to create a handwashing curriculum, and required few resources—each partner group received hand lotion costing under $10—and no simulation mannequins. Evaluation used paired pre/post surveys analyzed by paired t test, framed by the Kirkpatrick model.
requirements: A lecture room accommodating approximately 20 learners with tables for small-group interaction
A participant packet with a role-play exercise and theory reference sheet
Two faculty facilitators with procedural teaching experience
constraints: The "wide, not deep" generalizable approach may challenge learners with highly specialized procedural practices such as advanced endoscopy or invasive surgeries
Integrating multiple theories may confuse participants without background knowledge of educational theories
target_learners: medical residents and fellows from diverse specialties
target_learning_goals: apply Gagne's instructional design model to procedural skills teaching
apply Peyton's four-step model
define and apply deliberate practice
examples: Participants applied Gagne's model in small groups to create a handwashing curriculum using hand lotion to simulate hand sanitizer
key_sources: Smith Christopher J. MD, Rohlfsen Cory MD, Wardian Jana PhD, MSW, Sahak Khalid MD. (2024). Teaching Procedural Skills: Integrating Educational Theory Into Practice. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11476

article_title: Virtual versus jaw simulation in inlay preparation preclinical teaching: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Sheng Jie, Zhang Congdi, Gao Zhengkun, Yan Yimin, Meng Yucheng, Ren Shiqi, Liu Bin, Zhang Baoping. (2022). Virtual versus jaw simulation in inlay preparation preclinical teaching: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03930-6
title: UniDental-MU01 virtual simulation system for dental preparation training
description: A virtual simulation system (UniDental-MU01, UNIDRAW, China) used for preclinical inlay tooth preparation training, in which operators interact in real time with a 3D computer database and receive a scoring report after completing the preparation for every exercise. It provides "repeatable, recorded, and computerised training, which typically requires no supervision", saving teacher resources, and can simulate common and difficult clinical cases. Students rated its scores as accurate and its assessment items as perfect.
requirements: Computer interaction providing visual, auditory, and tactile sensory stimulation during training
constraints: It cannot perform fulcrum exercises for the operator and cannot simulate the oral clinical operation process
It has a slightly worse physical sense compared to the jaw model
Despite the high initial cost, it requires fewer consumables while being used more frequently
target_learning_goals: Dental preparation and restoration operative skills
examples: Each subject using the virtual system received the scoring report after completing the preparation for every exercise, and an analysis report of one subject is shown in the article's Fig. 2

article_title: Developing and validating a university needs instrument to measure the psychosocial needs of university students.
citation: Tindle, R., Castillo, P., Doring, N., Grant, L., & Willis, R. (2022). Developing and validating a university needs instrument to measure the psychosocial needs of university students. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 92, 1550–1570. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12515
title: University Needs Instrument (UNI)
description: The UNI is a 30-item self-report screening questionnaire measuring six psychosocial need areas of undergraduate students: academic, financial, family, friend, practical and emotional support, with five items per factor. "The UNI comprises 30 items within six identified areas of need, each consisting of five items." Each item begins with the stem 'I currently need…' and uses a five-point scale anchored by Strongly Disagree (1) and Strongly agree (5). The article reports excellent total-scale reliability (Cronbach's α = .94; McDonald's ω = .96) and initial validation evidence.
requirements: Administered as a survey with the sentence stem 'I currently need…' and a five-point rating scale from Strongly Disagree to Strongly agree
constraints: Initial validation only; the study did not test higher-order factor structure
Sample was largely first-year psychology students from a single country, so generalizability is limited per the authors
Data were collected during the Covid-19 pandemic
target_learning_goals: Identifying psychosocial support needs (academic, financial, family, friend, practical, emotional) to guide targeted university support services
examples: 511 undergraduates completed the UNI alongside the K10 in a cross-sectional Qualtrics survey during the 2021 teaching calendar
